title: Savannah blues singers and the medicine shows
summary: He recalls turpentine-field blues singers and the touring medicine shows with small bands, including clarinetist-comedian Wilton Crawley.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: And over there was where I met many of the old blues singers around there. Many of them didn't become famous but they worked in the turpentine fields around Savannah. Turpentine was a big thing that they had around there because ships would come in -- Savannah's a seaport -- and they would ship out this rosin and stuff that they would get from these trees.

But these guys were top blues singers, some of them around. They never got known. But then there are many bands that came through Savannah because it was right on that sea-board going from -- down to Florida. And the ministrel shows in the days I came up would come through there, shows like Dr. Rabbitfoot. These were where they had the old comedians, and these guys would sell medicine, the medicine shows. And they would make quite a bit of money from selling these -- this medicine. And there was no tax in those days. And they sold it.

But they would do a little show to attract people. They would put up a tent on a corner, and they didn't pay any rent for these corners. They'd just take a vacant lot and put these tents up. And they would attract quite a bit of attention. They all had bands, small orchestras with them, at least a drum, and a banjo, and perhaps some of them had a trombone player, maybe a trumpet player, and most had a clarinet player. One of the top clarinet players I ever met, Wilton Crawley, he

was a comedian, and he was also a clarinetist.

And he used to put a glass on his head, and he'd play the clarinet all between his legs, and do the splits and all. He was quite famous back in those days. And wherever he played on any of these medicine shows they were sure to have a big crowd.
